name: Dom zu St. Jakob Innsbruck
kurzbeschreibung: The baroque Dom zu St. Jakob in Innsbruck: built 1717–1724 by Johann Jakob Herkomer, Asam ceiling frescoes, Cranach's Mariahilf painting, and 48-bell carillon.
beschreibung:
Overview

The majestic Dom zu St. Jakob (also known as Innsbrucker Dom) forms the resplendent sacred heart of the Tyrolean provincial capital of Innsbruck. Situated on the quiet, cobblestoned Domplatz just steps away from the Imperial Hofburg and the Goldenes Dachl, the cathedral of the Diocese of Innsbruck rises as a triumphant masterpiece of High Baroque architecture. With its imposing twin-tower facade crafted from local Höttinger breccia, light-flooded domed vaults, and world-renowned artistic treasures, the cathedral attracts hundreds of thousands of pilgrims, worshippers, and cultural travellers from around the globe every year.

History & Architecture

First documented in 1180, the original Romanesque and later Gothic parish church served as an essential stop for pilgrims on the Way of St. James to Santiago de Compostela from the High Middle Ages onwards. After severe earthquakes in 1670 and 1689 caused heavy structural damage to the old building, the municipality commissioned a monumental reconstruction. Between 1717 and 1724, the present-day cathedral was built according to plans by the renowned Bavarian master builder Johann Jakob Herkomer; following his early death, his nephew Johann Georg Fischer completed the magnificent structure. For the interior decor, the celebrated Bavarian master artists Cosmas Damian Asam and Egid Quirin Asam were commissioned: Cosmas Damian created the eight monumental ceiling frescoes honouring the church patron St. James the Greater, while his brother Egid Quirin mastered the delicate stucco work and trompe-l'œil architecture. Presiding over the baroque high altar is the world-famous Mariahilf-Gnadenbild by Lucas Cranach the Elder (painted around 1537) – one of the most widely replicated depictions of the Virgin Mary in Christendom, donated solemnly in 1650 by Archduke Leopold V. In the left transept stands the monumental bronze tomb of Erzherzog Maximilian III. den Deutschmeister († 1618), designed after models by Hubert Gerhard and masterfully cast in 1620 by court founder Caspar Gras. In the north tower, the Mariahilf-Glockenspiel (Innsbruck Peace Carillon) by the Grassmayr bell foundry has rung since 1982: with 48 bells and a total weight of over four tonnes, it is the largest carillon in all of Austria.

Visit & Getting There

The Dom zu St. Jakob is open to visitors year-round: in the summer season (May to October) from Monday to Saturday from 10:15 to 19:30 and on Sundays and public holidays from 12:30 to 19:30; in the winter months (November to April) daily until 18:30 (sightseeing is not permitted during liturgical church services). Admission to the cathedral is free (donations for the upkeep of the church are requested; for private photography, a contribution fee of €1.00 is requested at the pamphlet stand). Getting there by public transport: from Innsbruck Hauptbahnhof, it is a leisurely 12-minute walk through the pedestrian zone; tram lines 1, 2, 3, and 5 stop at Terminal Marktplatz, and buses stop at Kongresshaus (both approx. three minutes' walk away). By car: parking is available in nearby underground parking garages, ideally the Altstadtgarage on Innrain or the Congressgarage.

Tips

The entire Domplatz and the entrance through the main portal are completely step-free and barrier-free for wheelchairs and prams; the nave is also accessible without thresholds. Every day punctually at 12:15, the Peace Carillon rings out with its 48 bells – take a seat on the benches facing the cathedral facade to enjoy the delicate melodies. Inside, make sure to admire the splendid baroque pulpit created by Nikolaus Moll in 1725, featuring the three allegorical figures of Faith, Hope, and Charity.
